{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mo-f","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"31f140d01a90dad73d89c50dcf5077ca079f4e860794d991f92ac19a932ea580","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mo-class-f:lineage:50","source_registry_sha256":"f128002157e581eb7004b9370c8cfbafd7b29a1596262980704fbda0a45932f5","source_liveness_sha256":"fdf72d02e75b9589fee5aaf5b83ec9705ff03586f574464e3553a827f9b698d8"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Missouri alcohol, drugs and driving: BAC limits, administrative and court penalties, Abuse and Lose, Minor in Possession, proof of insurance, chemical test refusal, ignition interlock, and the effects of alcohol, medicines and marijuana","heading":"C — Alcohol, drugs and driving: BAC limits, field and chemical tests, administrative versus court-convicted actions, penalty ladders, Abuse and Lose, Minor in Possession, SR-22 proof, refusal, ignition interlock, and how alcohol, medicines and marijuana impair driving","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Alcohol, drugs and driving: BAC limits, field and chemical tests, administrative versus court-convicted actions, penalty ladders, Abuse and Lose, Minor in Possession, SR-22 proof, refusal, ignition interlock, and how alcohol, medicines and marijuana impair driving
Knowledge domain: why impaired driving is dangerous, how an officer tests a suspected impaired driver, the legal blood alcohol limits, the two separate tracks of administrative and court-convicted penalties, the youth rules under Abuse and Lose and Minor in Possession, proof of insurance, what happens when you refuse a chemical test, when an ignition interlock device is required, and how alcohol, medicines and marijuana affect a driver.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol, drugs, even medicine, and being tired can all weaken your driving, and you are the one responsible for knowing when you are not fit to drive. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
Even a little alcohol may affect your driving, so if you plan to drink, hand the keys to someone who has not been drinking. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
If you injure or kill someone while driving after drinking or using drugs, you may face two to seven years in jail, a $5,000 fine, and/or losing your license for five years. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
An officer who suspects drinking may ask you to do field tests such as walking heel to toe or balancing on one leg, which help the officer decide whether to arrest you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
After an arrest, a chemical test of your breath, blood or urine gives your Blood Alcohol Content, called the BAC level. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
Missouri can act against an impaired driver in two separate ways, administrative actions and court-convicted actions, and each has its own penalties. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
If your BAC is .08% or more, or .02% or more for a minor, the officer takes your license and gives you a notice that it will be suspended or revoked after 15 days. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A01
That notice may include a 15-day driving permit if the officer marks it, and it lets you ask for a hearing or, if eligible, an immediate 90-day Restricted Driving Privilege. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A01
If you are granted a hearing, you may keep driving legally until 15 days after the decision is mailed to you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
On the administrative chart, a first offense brings a license suspension, and a second offense within a five-year period brings a one-year license revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Administrative entries marked with an asterisk require an Ignition Interlock Device to be installed before the license is reinstated. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
If a judge finds you guilty of DWI or of a BAC of .08% or more, you can no longer drive legally once the ticket reaches the Department, and you are told by mail when to stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
After a court conviction, your license is suspended, revoked or denied depending on your past driving record, and points are added to that record. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
A first DWI or BAC conviction can mean up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $500. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
A second DWI or BAC conviction can mean up to one year in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
A third DWI or BAC conviction can mean up to four years in jail and a fine of up to $5,000. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A02
A fourth DWI or BAC conviction can mean up to seven years in jail and a fine of up to $5,000. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A02
A fifth DWI or BAC offense can mean between five and 15 years in jail. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A02
For a first court-convicted offense the license is suspended for 90 days, and you may qualify for a 90-day or 60-day Restricted Driving Privilege. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A02
A second court-convicted offense brings a one-year revocation, while a second offense within five years brings a five-year license denial. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A02
A third court-convicted offense, and any later one, brings a ten-year license denial. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A03
Under the Abuse and Lose Law, a driver younger than 21 can lose the license for 90 days for any alcohol-related traffic offense, for having or using alcohol or drugs while driving, or for altering or misrepresenting a license. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A03
A driver under 18 who has or uses alcohol and is charged with a second offense can also lose the license for 90 days under Abuse and Lose. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A03
A driver aged 21 or older can lose the license for one year for having or using drugs while driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A03
To get the license back after that one-year loss, you pay a $45 fee, show you completed SATOP or a similar program, keep SR-22 proof of insurance for two years, and retake the full driver exam. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
A state court can suspend or revoke the license of someone older than 15 and under 21 for buying or trying to buy liquor, possessing it, being visibly intoxicated, or having a BAC above .02%. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A03
For a young person, drinking liquor counts as possessing it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A03
Minor in Possession penalties climb with each offense: a 30-day suspension, then a 90-day suspension, then a one-year revocation. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A03
After a Minor in Possession action you pay a $45 fee and attend SATOP or a similar program, and after a one-year revocation you also file SR-22 proof for two years and retake the driver exam. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A03
A driver facing DWI or BAC consequences must file proof of insurance with the Driver License Bureau, most often through an SR-22 insurance filing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A03
Proof of insurance must stay on file for two years; if it lapses, the license is suspended for the rest of that period unless you file again and pay a $20 fee. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A03
The one exception to the proof rule is a minor whose first offense is a BAC of .02% or more, who is not required to file it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A04
If you refuse a chemical test of your BAC when stopped by an officer, your license is taken away for one year. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A04
To be reinstated after an intoxication-related offense you pay a $45 fee, show SATOP or a similar program was completed, and keep SR-22 proof of insurance for two years. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A04
You must run an ignition interlock device on any vehicle you drive for at least six months after reinstatement if you had more than one intoxication-related contact, a BAC conviction of .15% or higher, or caused property damage or injury. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A04
An ignition interlock device is wired to the ignition, horn and headlights and checks breath alcohol, requiring a breath sample before the engine starts and at intervals while driving. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A04
The interlock must stay in place at least six months from reinstatement with no violations during the final three months, and you pay for its installation and its monthly service. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F38 | anchor: A04
A court conviction for failing to install a required interlock revokes your driving privilege for one year, and a second offense takes it away for five years. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F39 | anchor: A05
In Missouri you can be charged with DWI for driving impaired by alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription medicine, over-the-counter medicine, or any mix of them. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F40 | anchor: A05
Missouri law does not separate prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs, and DWI penalties are the same whether alcohol or drugs caused the impairment. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F41 | anchor: A05
It is illegal to drive with a BAC of 0.08% or more, with 0.04% for commercial vehicle drivers and 0.02% for drivers under 21. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F42 | anchor: A05
Even one drink will probably affect your driving, and in many cases two drinks could put you over the legal limit. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F43 | anchor: A05
All medicines, prescription or over-the-counter, can impair driving even when taken as directed, so ask your doctor or pharmacist and read the warning label. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F44 | anchor: A06
Marijuana is the drug cited second most often in car crashes, after alcohol. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F45 | anchor: A06
Missouri voters approved medical marijuana effective in 2020, yet driving under its influence is never legal or safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F46 | anchor: A06
Marijuana can impair thinking, judgment of time and distance, and coordination, and studies link it to more lane weaving and slower reactions. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

Misconceptions: a legal prescription or an over-the-counter medicine does not protect you from a DWI charge; DWI penalties are not lighter for drugs than for alcohol; medical marijuana approval does not make driving high legal; the administrative and court penalties are separate tracks, not one penalty; refusing the chemical test does not avoid a penalty.
Mnemonics: eight, four, two for the BAC limits from most drivers to commercial drivers to drivers under twenty-one; Abuse and Lose means abuse it and lose it.
Glossary: BAC means Blood Alcohol Content; DWI means Driving While Intoxicated; RDP means Restricted Driving Privilege; SATOP means Substance Awareness Traffic Offender Program; an SR filing means the insurance filing that proves coverage to the Driver License Bureau; IID means ignition interlock device; MIP means Minor in Possession.
Dynamic facts: fines, jail ranges, suspension lengths, BAC limits and reinstatement fees are statutory and can change, and the interlock installer list is kept by the transportation department.
